qt: to the Commission Sandro Ruotolo (S&D), Nicola Zingaretti (S&D) Subject:

Meta has agreed to a USD 16.7 billion settlement in a lawsuit brought against the company by a number of US states that had accused Facebook and Instagram of harming the well-being and mental health of underage users. This settlement has shed light on a situation of the utmost concern. Meta employees and witnesses revealed during the proceedings that the company kept certain underused protective measures in place and elected not to implement more effective alternatives because it did not want teenage users to spend less time on its platforms. This evidence only strengthens concerns that Meta is putting profits ahead of child safety. In the light of these developments and given that the Commission itself opened proceedings against Meta in May 2024 over child protection concerns, we ask the Commission: 1.
Over two years since it launched this investigation, how far along are its enquiries, and what conclusions have they reached so far?

Does the Digital Services Act give the Commission the power to compel Meta to introduce measures similar to the ones it has pledged to enforce in the US (time limits, night-time blocks et al), or would new legislation be needed to achieve this?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.11.2026) The Commission closely follows the recent settlement between Meta and US attorneygenerals. With the Digital Services Act (DSA)1, the EU has a legislative framework in place that applies, amongst others, to social media companies, which offer services in the EU and not only to those that are part of individual settlements. Some of the settlement’s measures are already in place in the EU through the DSA and its Guidelines on the Protection of Minors2, which detail the Commission’s expectations under the DSA and largely mirror the commitments agreed by Meta in the US. Meta is required to fully comply with these legislative tools. In this regard, the Commission has issued preliminary findings regarding Meta’s failure to implement effective age assurance3 as well as concerns about the addictive design of Instagram and Facebook4. The Commission continues these investigations as well as discussions with Meta on implementing any additional safeguards that may be needed for the protection of minors as required by the DSA. Furthermore, the Commission’s proposal for an EUKIDS Act – ‘EU Keeping Internet Digital Spaces Accountable and Trustworthy’5, which specifies the aforementioned Guidelines in law, provides clear dos and don’ts for all services in scope. For example, the proposal bans certain design features that encourage compulsive use.
1 Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 October 2022 on a Single
